summary: Jones Point Light (1856-1926) on the Potomac at the District of Columbia's southern corner, beside the 1791 boundary stone. Now in Jones Point Park, National Park Service.

structures.note: Cylindrical cast-iron lantern on a 1.5-story frame keeper's house, on a brick foundation. The USLHS record gives the tower as wood.

access.note: Jones Point Park, National Park Service. The USLHS record says open to the public; the building's interior is not confirmed in the sources read.

events.note: Alexandria Masonic Lodge placed a stone at the District's south corner on 15 April 1791 (NRHP).
Congressional appropriation of $5,000 to purchase land and erect a beacon at Jones Point, August 1852 (LighthouseFriends).
Tract of land bought from the Manassas Gap Railroad Company for $501 (LighthouseFriends); the Lighthouse Service Bulletin of 1926 dates the purchase to April 1855.
First lit 3 May 1856 by keeper George L. Deeton (LighthouseFriends); operated from 1856 (NPS).
Frame lighthouse building with lantern (USLHS; NPS). The NRHP dates the building to 1855.
Original fifth-order Fresnel lens (USLHS 1856; NRHP).
Lighthouse Board allowed an Alexandria gas company to extend gas lines to the station (LighthouseFriends).
Retaining wall built over the 1791 south cornerstone, which stayed covered until 1912 (NRHP).
Lamp converted to gas (NRHP).
Color of the light changed on 20 November 1900 (Lighthouse Board 1901); lamp reconverted to oil with a red chimney (NRHP).
Francis E. Wilkins took charge after Greenwood's death (LighthouseFriends; roster from 1906).
Commissioner of Lighthouses reports the station of little use because of shoreline change; proposes it may be discontinued once new range lights are established.
Massive shipyard built at Jones Point to build ships for World War I (NPS); the shipyard obscured the beacon.
Automatic flashing white acetylene light of 590 candlepower replaced the manually tended light (NRHP).
Anniversary program at the boundary stone, 15 April 1921 (NRHP). The 1921 Bulletin dates the Commissioner's visit to 13 April 1921.
Lighthouse put out of service in 1926 (NRHP; NPS).
Replaced by a 60-foot steel skeleton tower with a 200-candlepower acetylene light 100 yards east (NRHP).
Reservation declared surplus; transferred to the Mount Vernon Chapter of the DAR. Three sources give three forms of the transfer (act of Congress; revocable license; deed).
Army Signal Corps built a classified communication facility on the former shipyard and closed the site to the public (NPS).
Replacement light removed in the 1940s (NRHP).
Army reopened Jones Point to public entry; vandalism followed (NPS).
National Park Service acquired the area from the DAR; Jones Point Park opened (NRHP; NPS).

keepers.note: The NPS calls him the longest-serving keeper. LighthouseFriends says he kept the station 'for forty years' and counts four children by his first wife, Julia Savage (d. 1873), and seven by his second, Margaret Grover. The NPS says he had 14 children in all.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The NRHP dates the building to 1855. LighthouseFriends, the USLHS record and the NPS give 1856 for the light being lit or operating. The story keeps both.
The NRHP: the anniversary program was held on 15 April 1921. The 1921 Bulletin: the Commissioner visited on 13 April 1921 for the celebration. Both are given.

The NRHP: an act of Congress transferred the reservation to the DAR chapter. The 1926 Bulletin: the Department of Commerce granted a revocable license, pending possible legislation for permanent transfer. The NPS: deeded to the chapter. The story says the three accounts differ.
The roster lists Margaret Greenwood as acting principal keeper in 1906. LighthouseFriends says Francis E. Wilkins took charge after Greenwood's death. The story presents both.
The roster starts George L. Deeton in 1853; the light was first lit by him in May 1856 (LighthouseFriends). The roster date is probably his appointment, before the light was built.

LighthouseFriends counts 4 + 7 = 11 children by his two wives; the NPS says he had 14 children in all, and that 11 of them lived with his second wife in the house at one point. The story quotes the NPS figure as the NPS's own.

The NRHP says the 1791 stone was temporary and the permanent stone that replaced it in 1794 stands today in its apparent original location. An earlier draft called the 1794 stone 'the 1791 boundary stone' and 'the stone that marked the start of the survey'; the story now says the 1794 stone replaced the 1791 stone.

The NPS photograph caption gives 'Frank Wilkins, the last Jones Point Lighthouse keeper' (1912); the roster gives Francis E. Wilkins (1906-1918). No source states they are the same man; the story says the link is probable and not stated by a source.

notes_for_editor: 1. The keepers are from the USLHS roster (NARA registers via the Anderson inventory), whose heading is 'Principal Lighthouse Keeper'; normalised to 'head keeper'. Margaret Greenwood's acting role rests on the roster line alone. 2. The 1915 Commissioner report (scan p. 94, printed p. 89, fiscal 1915) and the 1926 and 1921 Bulletins (PDF pp. 22 and 18) were located through the corpus page index and read in the OCR text; the page images were not viewed. The 1921 Bulletin's 'On April 13, 1921' is legible in the OCR text. 3. The 1901 Lighthouse Board 'Color of light changed November 20, 1900' line is on printed page 16 (the page marker before it and the one after it bracket it). The volume has no archive.org page index, so the scan page (28 in the earlier draft) is not confirmed and was dropped from the footnote. 4. LighthouseFriends is a secondary account (all rights reserved); its prose is paraphrased and only one short phrase is quoted. Public-domain passages it reports are quoted as its quotations. 5. The 1857 Alexandria Gazette appropriations table lists 'Jones' point. Light-house' with a $5,000 sum, but the OCR is too damaged to quote, so it is not used. 6. Wikipedia (lead only) says the light was relit by a private concern in 1995 and then put out again after the change of owner. Not verified; not in the story. 7. The NRHP says the 1926 replacement tower stood until the 1940s; the NPS says the replacement was removed later, and the Wikipedia lead says ten years. The story uses only the NRHP's 1940s. 8. The 1980 NRHP nomination is the source for the stone's present condition; the story dates it to the nomination. 9. Living people: none named. Benjamin Banneker and Andrew Ellicott are historical figures named through the NRHP.
